title: The Four Ways to Pay in Cambodia, Ranked by How Much They Annoy You
summary: Cash, foreign cards, local Bakong wallets, or scanning KHQR with Moreta Pay: an honest comparison of how travelers and expats actually pay in Cambodia in 2026.
body_markdown:
Buy a bottle of water in Phnom Penh and you will get a fast lesson in Cambodian money. The price is in dollars, you pay in dollars, and your change comes back as a handful of riel notes you have never seen before. Was that the right amount? Probably. Will you ever spend those small notes before they disintegrate in your pocket? Unclear.


Cambodia runs on two currencies at once, US dollars for bigger amounts and Khmer riel for everything small, and the mental overhead of that is the main reason visitors find money here confusing. The good news is that the country also has one of the cleanest QR payment systems in Southeast Asia. The question is how you, a person without a Cambodian bank account, actually get into it.


Here are the four real options, weighed honestly.


## Option one: cash, the default that never quite works


Cash still works everywhere in Cambodia, from Angkor ticket counters to the smallest village shop. That is its entire case, and it is a genuinely strong one. No app, no signal, no battery required.


The problems are all in the details. First, the dual currency. Dollars are accepted almost everywhere, but torn, marked, or old-series US notes often get refused, so you end up inspecting your own money like a bank teller. Second, change. Anything under a dollar comes back in riel, which means that within three days you are carrying a wad of 100, 500, and 1,000 riel notes that most visitors never learn to count at speed. Tuk tuk drivers rarely have change for larger dollar bills, and asking a market vendor to break a twenty for a two dollar purchase is a small social negotiation every single time.


Third, getting the cash. Cambodian ATMs dispense dollars, which is convenient, but between your home bank's foreign withdrawal fee and the ATM's own fee, every cash run has a cost, and you are back on the ATM treadmill you were hoping to escape.


**Verdict:**


necessary as a backup, exhausting as a primary method.


## Option two: your foreign card, useful in a narrow lane


Visa and Mastercard work fine at the places built for foreigners: hotels, larger restaurants in Phnom Penh and Siem Reap, supermarkets, some pharmacies. If your trip consists entirely of those places, a good no-foreign-fee card covers you.


Step outside that lane and the card stops mattering. The noodle stall, the fruit vendor, the barber, the laundry shop, the tuk tuk driver, the guesthouse owner who gives you the better nightly rate: none of them have a card terminal, and most never will, because the QR code taped to their counter does the job for free. Some smaller businesses that do take cards add a surcharge for the privilege, and dynamic currency conversion at hotel desks quietly worsens your rate if you are not paying attention.


**Verdict:**


keep it for hotels and emergencies, but it will not make you feel like you live here.


## Option three: a local Bakong wallet, the real thing you mostly cannot have


What locals actually use is[KHQR](https://moretapay.com/networks/khqr) , the national QR standard built on the Bakong system run through Cambodia's central bank infrastructure. One QR format, accepted by essentially every bank and wallet app in the country. A Phnom Penh office worker pays for coffee, rent, a motorbike wash, and a Shopee order through the same scan-and-confirm motion, often through apps like ABA or Wing, and the amounts settle in riel or dollars without anyone handling small notes.


It is a genuinely excellent system, and the catch for you is simple: joining it the local way means opening a Cambodian bank account or wallet, which typically wants local ID, a local phone number, sometimes proof of address, and a visit to a branch. For an expat settling in long term with the right visa, that can be worth doing. For a traveler on a few weeks, or a nomad on a three month stint, it is paperwork for a payment method you will abandon at the border.


Even nomads who manage to open something often hit a second snag: funding it. Moving money from a foreign bank into a Cambodian account involves international transfers that cost more than the convenience is worth. We covered the funding problem in more depth in our piece on


[how to fund a KHQR payment app without a local account](https://moretapay.com/blog/how-to-fund-a-khqr-payment-app-for-cambodia-without-opening-a-local-account)


.


**Verdict:**


the best system in the country, locked behind residency-shaped doors.


## Option four: scanning KHQR with Moreta Pay


This is the newer path: keep your home bank, skip the Cambodian account, and scan the same KHQR codes locals scan. Moreta Pay works like this in practice. You top up a wallet in your own currency from your home bank (US bank via Plaid or ACH, SEPA in Europe, UK Faster Payments, Canadian e-Transfer) or from an international card. At the noodle stall, you scan the laminated KHQR code on the counter, see the amount, the merchant's name, and the exact exchange rate on screen, and confirm. The vendor's phone pings, the vendor nods, done.


What this quietly fixes is the dual currency confusion. You never have to decide whether to hand over dollars or riel, never count unfamiliar small notes, and never do the mid-transaction math of a dollar price with riel change. The app shows one clear number before you commit, and the conversion happens behind the scenes with no hidden foreign transaction fee layered on top. The same approach works for QR checkouts online, so booking a Siem Reap guesthouse on Agoda or ordering from a Cambodian seller works the same way as the street stall.


Honest caveats, because this is a comparison and not an ad. You need a data connection to scan, so sort out connectivity early (here is


[whether you actually need a local SIM to pay by QR](https://moretapay.com/blog/do-digital-nomads-in-malaysia-and-cambodia-need-a-local-sim-to-pay-by-qr)


). You should top up before you are hungry, not while the soup is getting cold. And a thin layer of cash is still wise for the rare stall with a faded, unscannable code or a countryside stop where the owner's phone is charging somewhere in the back.


**Verdict:**


the local system without the local paperwork, with a small battery-and-signal dependency as the price.


## So what does a sensible setup look like?


Ranked by annoyance, from worst to best, for a typical visitor in 2026:


- **Cash as your main method:**


works everywhere but taxes you constantly in riel-counting, note-inspecting, and ATM runs.


- **Foreign card only:**


fine in the tourist lane, useless the moment Cambodia gets interesting.


- **Opening a local wallet:**


the ideal endpoint for permanent residents, an unreasonable project for everyone else.


- **KHQR through Moreta Pay, plus a small cash float:**


the combination that covers roughly everything with the least friction.


Cambodia rewards visitors who adopt local habits quickly, and the QR habit is the easiest one to pick up. Scan, check the name and the rate, confirm, keep walking.


[Set up Moreta Pay before you land](https://moretapay.com/?utm_source=blog&utm_medium=article&utm_campaign=country-seo)


and the first KHQR code you meet, probably at a coffee cart outside the airport, will already feel routine.
